title: Mesoscopic Quantum Communication via Photon-Number Moments
authors: Gabriele Cenedese, Alex Pozzoli, Luca Razzoli, Alessia Allevi
abstract: Mesoscopic optical states are a promising resource for quantum communication, combining robustness against losses with the preservation of genuine quantum features. Here, we propose a quantum communication protocol in which information is encoded in the first and second moments of the photon-number distributions of classical optical states, and then decoded by photon-number-resolving detectors. Security relies on the nonclassical photon-number correlations of a twin-beam state transmitted alongside the signal in the quantum channel, providing an experimentally accessible security witness against both intercept-resend and beam-splitter attacks investigated in this work. Numerical simulations performed in experimentally accessible parameter regimes support the feasibility and security of the proposed communication protocol, yielding nonzero key generation rates under the considered eavesdropping attacks, and motivating its future experimental implementation.
summary: The authors propose a secure quantum communication protocol using mesoscopic optical states encoded via the first and second moments of photon number distributions. Security is guaranteed by utilizing the nonclassical correlations present in an accompanying twin-beam state resource against common eavesdropping attacks. The numerical simulations confirm that this approach maintains key generation rates, suggesting feasibility for future experimental realization.
main_problem: To propose a quantum communication protocol that enhances robustness against photon loss by encoding information in mesoscopic optical states.
main_result: The protocol is shown to be secure against intercept-resend and beam-splitting attacks, yielding non-zero key generation rates under numerical simulation.
method: Information is encoded using the first and second moments of photon-number distributions ($\langle n angle$ and $	ext{Var}(n)$) of classical states superimposed on a twin-beam state.
model_or_system: The system utilizes mesoscopic optical states, specifically multi-mode twin-beam (TWB) states generated via spontaneous parametric down-conversion, requiring Photon-Number-Resolving (PNR) detectors for implementation.
key_observables: Photon-number moments ($\langle n angle$, $	ext{Var}(n)$), the noise reduction factor ($R$), and the Key Generation Rate (KGR).
important_parameters: Mesoscopic intensity regime, detection efficiency ($\eta=0.4$), TWB mean photon number ($\langle m_{Alice} angle$ in $[3.0, 10.0]$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the use of PNR detectors and that security relies on exploiting nonclassical correlations inherent to the twin-beam resource.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates photon number distributions and variances for various pseudo-thermal states versus $\langle n angle$. Figure 2 sketches the proposed communication scheme alongside models for intercept-resend and beam-splitting attacks.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by proposing an encoding based on moments, derives security witnesses using TWB correlations ($R<1$), analyzes performance metrics (TPR, KGR) against specific eavesdropping attacks, and concludes with feasibility statements for experimental implementation.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum key distribution in a high-loss regime by leveraging classical state properties combined with nonclassical entanglement resources, which is highly relevant to practical quantum networking research.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Photon number distributions of the multi-mode pseudo-thermal state (mTh), single-mode pseudo-thermal state (Th), super-thermal state from a speckled-speckle field (sTh), and second-harmonic of single-mode pseudo-thermal state (sTh2), all of them having a mean value ⟨n⟩= 0.45, µs = 1 for Th, STh and STh2, while µs = 10 for mTh, and µs2 = 1 for STh. (b) Variance as a function of the mean value for the same states as in panel (a); the vertical dashed line highligths ⟨n⟩= 0.45.

FIG. 2. (a) Sketch of the proposed communication scheme, where Alice encodes information into classical optical states of light with different photon-number distributions and sends them to Bob through a quantum channel together with the portion of a TWB state. Sketch of (b) the IR attack and (c) the BS attack performed by Eve. In (b) α is the fraction of data corresponding to a given symbol intercepted and replaced by Eve, while in (c) t is the transmissivity of the BS and (1 −t) its reflectivity.

FIG. 3. (a) Bob’s discrimination accuracies ACCσ2, ACCR, and p(R > 1) as a function of the data sample size dsample per symbol, for loss ∆= 0.5 and mean photon number of the TWB ⟨mAlice⟩= 5. (b) Bob’s ACCσ2 and p(R > 1) as a function of ⟨mAlice⟩, for dsample = 2 × 104 and varying ∆. In both panels, blue tones refer to ACC, while brown tones refer to p(R > 1). The superimposed signals have mean values ⟨ms,L⟩= 0.40 and ⟨ms,H⟩= 0.45.

FIG. 4. (a) Bob’s discrimination accuracy ACCσ2 as a function of the fraction of intercepted data α in the IR attack and (b) as a function of the BS reflectivity (1 −t) in the BS attack. Different colors and line styles correspond to different classifiers: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN), Linear Support Vector Machine (SVMlinear), Support Vector Machine with Radial Basis Function kernel (SVMRBF), Logistic Regression (LR), Random Forest (RF), and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). In all panels the parameters are ⟨ms,L⟩= 0.40, ⟨ms,H⟩= 0.45, ⟨mAlice⟩= 5, ∆= 0.5, and dsample = 2 × 104.

FIG. 5. Bob’s (dots) and Eve’s (open circles) discrimination accuracy ACCσ2 as a function of (a) α in the IR attack and (b) (1 −t) in the BS attack. The dashed line indicates the accuracy of the random classifier, namely ACC = 1/8. Security-related figures of merit based on the noise reduction factor R are the probability that Bob measures nonclassical correlations p(R < 1) (asterisks) and the TPRR (stars). In both panels, the parameters are ⟨ms,L⟩= 0.40, ⟨ms,H⟩= 0.45, ⟨mAlice⟩= 5, ∆= 0.5, and dsample = 2 × 104.
